name: Gareth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Millbrook depot by half six, kettle on, and the crew leader, Dev, reads out the job sheets. Most days it's overhead work on the rural network: changing rotten poles, restringing a span a tractor took down, swapping a cracked insulator. I've done this thirty-nine years, since I was nineteen and an apprentice, so I don't need telling twice. What wears me out now is the knees and the paperwork, in that order.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, after all those years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The moment the power comes back on. You're up a pole in the rain at two in the morning, you close the switch, and a whole valley of kitchen windows lights up at once. Nobody sees you do it, and I like that. My wife Ruth says I'm the only man she knows who's proud of being invisible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for three years: told you so. At the depot we'd have a laugh about the office lot who were told they'd be replaced by a chatbot. I'm not online much, but I'd probably say it to my brother-in-law at Sunday dinner, because he's the one who keeps sending me articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that suits me. I've got about four years to go until I can take my pension at sixty-two, and I want them to be boring. The only thing I'd watch is the company using "AI" as an excuse to squeeze the crews anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd turn up, do the job, go to the union branch meeting on the first Tuesday like always. Ruth and I would keep putting a bit by and planning the camper van trip to the coast for when I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything. Like getting the all-clear from the doctor on something you weren't that worried about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the company using AI as an excuse. Have you seen that happen already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. Last spring they brought in a new scheduling system and in the same breath said the depot could run with two fewer fitters. Nobody said AI out loud, but the manager kept saying "smart planning", which is the same thing in a nicer coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they did try to cut crews and blame AI anyway, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's a union fight, same as any other. In 2019 they tried to cut us from four-man crews to three on live work, and we stopped it because it isn't safe. A computer program being hype or not doesn't change what's safe up a pole.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the depot and my brother-in-law that I called it, and that the hype was always for the office crowd. I'm not one for posting online, so it would be a laugh over Sunday dinner.
S0.think: I think it means nothing changes for me, and I'm glad, because I want my last four years before my pension at sixty-two to be boring. My one worry is the company using AI as cover to squeeze the crews anyway.
S0.do: Keeps working his normal shifts at the Millbrook depot and keeps going to the first-Tuesday union branch meeting. Carries on saving with Ruth for a camper van trip when he retires.
S0.feel: Relieved and settled, like a clean check-up. A small edge of suspicion about the bosses.
S0.quote: A computer program being hype or not doesn't change what's safe up a pole.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth treats AI mainly as a new label for an old fight about crew sizes and safety. He is financially secure and close to his pension, so the plateau barely registers. The 2019 crew-size dispute is clearly a defining memory and shapes how he reads every change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to get ahead of it, and I'd say it loudly at branch. We'd want it in the agreement that nothing replaces a person on live work without a proper safety review. I'd still be the one rolling my eyes when the trainer shows us a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm too close to the end for it to really touch me, and I know that's a bit selfish. The ones I'd worry about are the control room staff and the planners, because that's thinking work, not climbing work. And young Kyle, our apprentice, who's got forty years ahead of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd push for a motion at the branch meeting asking for a written deal on new tech: no job cuts without talks, training paid for in work time. If they bring in some fault-finding app on the tablets, I'd let Dev or Kyle drive it and I'd do the climbing. Money-wise, nothing changes; Ruth and I already have more than a year of spending put by and the house is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my mortgage, there isn't one, but for the place. I don't like the feeling of the ground shifting under the people coming after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Kyle. What would you say to him if he asked whether to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him stay. Somebody still has to climb the pole when the app says the fault's at pole 212, and it's never quite at pole 212. But I'd tell him to learn the gadgets too, because he's young and he can, and I can't be bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company made it part of your job to use one of these tools, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it as little as I could get away with. I've seen three "new systems" in my time, and every one of them meant more boxes to tick and less time on the actual job. If it came to it I'd ask Kyle to show me once, write it on a card, and keep the card in my hard hat.

S1.say: At branch I'd say the union has to get ahead of this and get a written deal so nothing replaces a person on live work without a safety review. I'd still roll my eyes at the new apps.
S1.think: I think I'm too close to the end for it to really touch me, and I know that's a bit selfish. The ones I'd worry about are the control room and planning staff, and young apprentices like Kyle.
S1.do: Puts a motion to his union branch asking for a written new-technology agreement with no cuts without talks and training in work time. Leaves any new fault-finding app to younger crew members and keeps his finances as they are, with over a year of spending saved and no mortgage.
S1.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, mostly on behalf of the younger ones and the depot as a place.
S1.quote: I'd ask Kyle to show me once, write it on a card, and keep the card in my hard hat.
S1.fieldNote: His instinct is collective: the first move is a branch motion, not anything personal. He openly admits he is shielded by age and savings, and his concern points outward to apprentices and office staff. His resistance to tools is practical and stubborn rather than fearful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that it was allowed to happen with no plan, and I'd say it at every meeting I could get to. I'd say the government should have stepped in, and that the companies making these things should be paying for the mess. I might even write to our MP, which I've done exactly once before, about the hospital closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm sixty and the pension doesn't start till sixty-two. So I'm two years short, and that worries me, even with the savings. And if robots are up poles by then, I'd be sick about what happens to the lads, the trade, the whole depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd go to the branch and say we need a fight on two fronts: protection for the young ones and early pension access for the older ones without a penalty. I'd sit down with Ruth and work out whether we can bridge two years on the savings, and I think we could if we skip the camper van. Once it arrives, if they offer voluntary redundancy, I'd take it and go, because I won't be the one teaching a robot my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach turn. I'd be losing sleep over it, and not much does that to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's talk about the time. With only two years' warning, what can't you do that you'd want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't ride it out to my proper pension date, that's the main thing. And I can't help Kyle or the other apprentices find their feet somewhere else, because there won't be anywhere else that a robot isn't also heading for. Two years is nothing. It's two winters of storms and then it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't teach a robot your job. What if they asked you to, for extra pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not for any money. I'd rather sit on my savings for two years than help put the lads out of work. Ruth would probably tell me I'm being daft, and she might be right, but that's where I stand.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace it was allowed to happen with no plan and that the companies behind it should pay for the mess. I'd say it at every meeting I could and maybe write to my MP.
S2.think: I think two years leaves me at sixty, two years short of my pension, and that worries me even with savings. I'd be sick about what happens to the young lads, the trade and the whole depot.
S2.do: Pushes his union branch to campaign for protection for apprentices and penalty-free early pension access for older workers. Works out with Ruth how to bridge two years on savings, dropping the camper van plan, and takes voluntary redundancy if it's offered.
S2.feel: Sick to his stomach and losing sleep, which he says almost never happens to him.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. It's two winters of storms and then it's gone.
S2.fieldNote: This is the first scenario where his own plans crack: the gap between sixty and his pension at sixty-two becomes real. He still frames his response through the union and the government, and blames the companies building the technology. His refusal to train a robot is a matter of pride, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse this time for not having a plan. I'd be on at the union and anyone in government who'd listen to get a proper transition deal in writing. I'd say it at work, mostly, because that's where people actually listen to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years takes me to sixty-three, so I'd get my pension. That's the honest truth, and it makes a big difference. But it doesn't fix the feeling of watching the trade I gave my life to get switched off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd stay on the tools and keep my head down to reach sixty-two. I'd put more into savings now, maybe an extra two hundred a month, in case the company starts offering worse terms near the end. And I'd go to every union meeting about the transition, because the deal they make in those five years decides what Kyle's lot get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's the difference between being pushed off a ladder and climbing down it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said two years made you sick. What changes with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it's the pension. With two years I'm scrambling, with five I'm already out the door on my full pension by the time it lands. It also gives the union time to fight properly instead of just picking up the pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hannah she's probably fine, she's a physio and people still want a person's hands on their bad back. My son Owen drives buses, and I'd tell him to start looking now, while he's got five years, not two. I'd hate saying it, because I always told him a steady job was the best thing you can have.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse this time for not having a plan. I'd be on at the union and anyone in government to get a proper transition deal in writing.
S3.think: I think five years gets me to my pension, which honestly makes a big difference. But it doesn't fix the feeling of watching the trade I gave my life to get switched off.
S3.do: Stays on the tools to reach his pension at sixty-two and adds about two hundred a month to savings in case terms get worse. Attends every union meeting on the transition deal for younger workers.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to breathe, more in control than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being pushed off a ladder and climbing down it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter hugely to him because they cover his pension date. His worry shifts from his own money to his son Owen and the apprentices. He still won't change his own work habits; his only new action is saving more and staying involved in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so do it properly. Retrain the young ones, protect the pensions, keep a person in charge of anything live. I'd still be saying it at branch, though I'd be gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's over the horizon. I'll be sixty-eight and in a camper van, I hope. It's the country I'd be thinking about, and whether my grandkids grow up in a place where nobody climbs anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as planned and retire at sixty-two. In the meantime, I'd back the union pushing for a training fund so the young lads can move into something, whatever that turns out to be. I wouldn't learn any of it myself, I'll be honest, there's no point at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for me, uneasy for the others. A bit sad, like seeing your old school get knocked down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for making that ten years count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that build it and the government, together. They're the ones getting rich and they're the ones who are meant to look after people. The union can push, but it can't pay for a training college on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything ten years would let you do that you'd want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to do some training at the college before I go, teaching climbing and safety to apprentices. Even if robots end up doing the work, somebody has to know how it's done properly. Maybe that's me being stubborn, but I'd want the knowledge written down by people who did it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so do it properly: retrain the young ones, protect pensions, keep a person in charge of anything live. I'd say it at branch even though I'd be gone by then.
S4.think: I think it's over the horizon for me, since I'll be sixty-eight and retired. What I'd really be thinking about is whether my grandkids grow up somewhere nobody climbs anything.
S4.do: Keeps working to retire at sixty-two as planned and backs the union's push for a training fund for younger workers. Does not learn the new tools himself, and hopes to teach climbing and safety at the college before he leaves.
S4.feel: Calm for himself, uneasy for others, and a little sad, like watching his old school come down.
S4.quote: Even if robots end up doing the work, somebody has to know how it's done properly.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he is personally safe and says so plainly. The sadness here is about the trade's knowledge being lost, which is why he wants to teach before he goes. He holds firm on not learning the new tools himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It lands right in the gap before my pension and it gives nobody any time, not me, not Kyle, not the company. What would help is being able to take my pension early with no penalty, and a proper plan for the young ones that's agreed with the union, not just announced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety, and that's the thing I'd want written down. Whatever goes up a pole, a person has to be able to say stop. I've seen what eleven thousand volts does to a man, and I'm not trusting a computer to know when to say stop.

headlineQuote: I've seen what eleven thousand volts does to a man, and I'm not trusting a computer to know when to say stop.
portrait: Gareth is a 58-year-old overhead lineworker at a rural depot who has climbed poles for thirty-nine years and is counting down to his pension at sixty-two. He's a lifelong union man who never touches AI tools and sees every new system through the lens of crew sizes and safety. With the house paid off and over a year of savings, the plateau and steady change barely touch him, though he worries for his apprentice Kyle and his bus-driver son. The two-year AGI picture is the one that hits hard, landing in the gap before his pension, while five and ten years let him climb down the ladder rather than be pushed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands two years before his pension and gives nobody, including the young apprentices, any time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take his pension early with no penalty, and a plan for young workers agreed with the union rather than simply announced.
